cards.title: The Great Stink that gave London its sewers
cards.body:
In the summer of 1858, hot weather turned the River Thames into an open sewer. For years, London's waste had poured straight into the river, the same river much of the city drew drinking water from. The stench reached the Houses of Parliament on the riverbank, where curtains were reportedly soaked in chemicals to mask it.

With politicians unable to ignore the problem, Parliament quickly backed a plan by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette. Over the following years his team built a vast network of intercepting sewers that carried waste east, away from central London.

The system also helped end the cholera outbreaks that had killed tens of thousands of Londoners. Many people still blamed bad air for the disease, but the physician John Snow had already linked cholera to contaminated water in 1854.
cards.example: Bazalgette is said to have made his pipes far wider than his calculations required, reasoning that the city would only get one chance to build them. Parts of his network still carry London's sewage today, and the Victoria Embankment along the Thames was built partly to house it.
cards.takeaway: Crisis made the case: the Great Stink turned a known problem into action.

cards.title: The Romanian deadlift: hinge, don't squat
cards.body:
The Romanian deadlift (RDL) is one of the best exercises for the hamstrings and glutes, and it teaches the hip hinge, the movement behind deadlifts, kettlebell swings and safely lifting anything off the floor.

Start standing tall, holding a barbell or dumbbells at your thighs. With a soft bend in your knees, push your hips straight back, as if closing a car door behind you with your backside. Keep the bar close, sliding it down your thighs, and keep your back flat. Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings, usually somewhere around mid-shin, then drive your hips forward to stand.

The most common mistake is turning it into a squat by bending the knees too much. In an RDL, the knees stay mostly fixed and the hips do the moving.
cards.example: This week, add RDLs after squats: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps with a weight that leaves two reps in reserve. Film one set from the side; your shins should stay nearly vertical and the bar should stay close to your legs the whole way.
cards.takeaway: In an RDL, the hips move back and forward; the knees barely change.

cards.title: TFSA withdrawals: why timing matters
cards.body:
The TFSA's flexibility is one of its best features: you can withdraw money at any time, tax-free, for any reason. But one rule catches many people. The amount you withdraw is added back to your contribution room only on January 1 of the following year, not immediately.

If you withdraw and then re-contribute in the same calendar year without enough unused room, the extra counts as an overcontribution. The CRA charges a tax of 1% per month on the highest excess amount in each month until it's removed.

So think of a withdrawal as returning room next year. And if you want to move your TFSA from one institution to another, don't withdraw and redeposit; ask the new institution for a direct transfer, which doesn't affect your room at all.
cards.example: You've used all your room. In March you withdraw $3,000 for a trip, then in June you put the $3,000 back. That's an overcontribution until January 1, costing about $30 for each month it stays in from June to December, roughly $210. Waiting until January would have cost nothing.
cards.takeaway: TFSA withdrawals come back as room next January, not right away.

cards.title: Fibre: the nutrient most people quietly miss
cards.body:
Protein gets all the attention, but fibre is the nutrient most adults fall short on. Health Canada's adequate intake for adults under 50 is 38 grams a day for men and 25 for women, and typical diets land well below that.

Fibre is the part of plant foods your body can't digest. Soluble fibre, found in oats, beans and lentils, forms a gel that slows digestion and can help lower LDL cholesterol. Insoluble fibre, found in whole grains and vegetable skins, adds bulk and keeps digestion regular. Both feed the bacteria in your gut, which turn some fibre into compounds that help keep the gut lining healthy.

A vegetarian diet makes this easier, since beans, lentils, whole grains, nuts and seeds are all fibre-rich. Increase it gradually, and drink more water as you do.
cards.example: A day that clears 38 g: oatmeal with raspberries and chia (about 15 g), lentil soup at lunch (about 10 g), an apple (about 4 g), and a black bean and vegetable burrito bowl at dinner (about 12 g).
cards.takeaway: Most people need more fibre; beans, oats and whole grains close the gap.

cards.title: The F barre chord without the pain
cards.body:
The F barre chord is where many guitarists give up, but it depends more on technique than strength. The shape is an open E major chord moved up one fret, with your index finger laid across all six strings at the first fret, acting as a new nut.

Three adjustments make it work. Roll your index finger slightly onto its bony outer edge, which presses more evenly than the soft underside. Keep the barre right behind the fret wire, not in the middle of the fret. And instead of squeezing with your thumb, let the weight of your arm pull the neck gently back toward you.

Pick each string one at a time to find the dead ones, and adjust. Expect a week or two of buzzing; that's normal. Once it rings, sliding the shape up the neck gives you every major chord.
cards.example: Practise for five minutes a day: form the F barre at the first fret, strum, release, and repeat 20 times. If the first fret is too tough, start the same shape at the fifth fret, which is A major and needs less pressure, then work your way down.
cards.takeaway: A barre chord is technique, not grip strength: roll, place, use arm weight.

cards.title: Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time
cards.body:
In 1955, the historian C. Northcote Parkinson published a satirical essay in The Economist that opened with a line that has stuck ever since: work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion. Give yourself a week for a task that needs two hours, and it will somehow take the week.

He was mocking bloated bureaucracies, but the idea fits personal work too. Long deadlines invite procrastination, perfectionism and scope creep, while tight ones force you to decide what actually matters.

The practical fix is to set your own shorter deadlines. Timebox tasks: decide in advance that you'll spend 45 minutes on a problem set or a first draft, set a timer, and stop when it rings. You'll often find the work fits, and the parts you skipped weren't essential.
cards.example: You have a case study due in five days. Instead of letting it hover all week, block two 90-minute sessions for tomorrow and the day after, aiming for a complete draft by the end of the second. Use the remaining days only for revisions.
cards.takeaway: Shrink the time you allow, and the work usually shrinks with it.

quiz.question: What finally pushed Parliament to back London's modern sewer system?
options: A royal decree from Queen Victoria
A fire that destroyed the old drains
The Great Stink of 1858 reaching Parliament itself
A loan from the Bank of England
quiz.explanation: When the stench of the Thames reached the Houses of Parliament, politicians quickly backed Bazalgette's sewer plan.

quiz.question: What's the most common mistake in the Romanian deadlift?
options: Bending the knees too much and turning it into a squat
Keeping the bar too close to the legs
Pushing the hips back
Keeping the back flat
quiz.explanation: The RDL is a hinge: the hips travel back and forward while the knees stay mostly fixed.

quiz.question: You withdraw $5,000 from your TFSA in April. When is that $5,000 of room restored?
options: Immediately
After 30 days
On your next birthday
On January 1 of the following year
quiz.explanation: Withdrawals are added back to your contribution room at the start of the next calendar year.

quiz.question: Which type of fibre forms a gel and can help lower LDL cholesterol?
options: Insoluble fibre from vegetable skins
Soluble fibre from oats, beans and lentils
Fibre added to protein powder
There is only one type of fibre
quiz.explanation: Soluble fibre forms a gel in digestion, which slows it down and can help lower LDL cholesterol.

quiz.question: What's the best way to hold down a barre without excessive squeezing?
options: Roll onto the index finger's bony edge, place it right behind the fret, and use arm weight
Press hard with the thumb on the back of the neck
Place the barre in the middle of the fret
Use the soft underside of the finger
quiz.explanation: Finger position and arm weight do the work that beginners try to do with thumb strength.

quiz.question: Given Parkinson's law, what's a practical way to finish work faster?
options: Wait for motivation before starting
Give each task as much time as possible
Set shorter, self-imposed deadlines and timebox the work
Multitask across several projects
quiz.explanation: If work expands to fill the time available, the fix is to make less time available.
